opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's actually really valuable, and it's something we've leaned into more over time. One of the persistent worries about a survey like ours is that when you ask a few thousand AI researchers, "When will unaided machines be able to accomplish every task better and more cheaply than human workers?", you don't really know what's going on in their heads when they answer. Are they picturing the same thing we're picturing? Are they thinking about physical tasks, or just cognitive ones? Do they take "unaided" seriously? Are they answering in thirty seconds because they want to get through the survey?

So asking people afterward how they understood a question, or including follow-ups that probe their interpretation, gives you a check on whether the numbers mean what you think they mean. And sometimes what you learn is a bit humbling. We've seen for a long time that framing makes a big difference. If you ask about "high-level machine intelligence," meaning all tasks, versus "full automation of labor," meaning all occupations, you get forecasts that are decades apart, even though logically those should be pretty close. That gap is itself evidence that people aren't working through a consistent model when they answer. Interpretation questions help you work out whether it's a real disagreement about the world or just people reading the questions differently.

I'd also say it's useful for being honest about what the survey is. I don't think of it as a source of precise forecasts. Researchers aren't necessarily good forecasters, and the inconsistencies show that. But it's still really important to know what the people building this technology believe, or at least what they say when asked, including how worried they are about extinction-level outcomes, how fast they expect things to move, and so on. Knowing how they interpreted the questions lets you report that more faithfully. You can say, "Here's what they said, here's roughly what they took us to mean, and here's how much weight we think that can bear."

So for me it's a mix of quality control and actually learning something about how experts think about these questions, which is interesting in its own right.

r001.rationale: The response says interpretation follow-ups check whether survey answers mean what researchers think they mean and help determine whether confusing forecast gaps reflect genuine disagreement or respondents reading the questions differently.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually one of the more underrated parts of the whole exercise. When you ask something like "when will high-level machine intelligence arrive," you're assuming the people answering have a shared picture of what you mean, and it turns out that's just not true. We found huge framing effects, for instance, between asking about "high-level machine intelligence" versus "full automation of labor," even though on paper those are pointing at roughly the same thing. People gave answers that differed by decades. So clearly the words are doing a lot of work, and not always the work we intended.

So asking respondents how they interpreted the question is partly a diagnostic tool. It tells you which of your numbers you should trust and which ones are really measuring something closer to "what mood does this phrasing put me in." If a lot of people say, "well, I read 'all tasks' as meaning the economically important ones," or "I assumed you meant it would be cheaper than a human," then you learn that the headline forecast is bundling together several different claims, and you can start to pull those apart.

It also keeps us honest about what a survey like this can and can't do. These are not people who have spent weeks thinking carefully about timelines. Most of them spend maybe ten or fifteen minutes on it, and they're drawing on intuitions rather than models. I think the results are still informative, because this is the population that's actually building the technology, and their collective intuition is a real signal. But it's a signal about their beliefs, including whatever confusions they carry, not an oracle. Asking about interpretation is how you figure out what the beliefs actually were.

And then there's a more forward-looking reason, which is that we want future surveys to be better. If we learn that a particular term is ambiguous, we can either define it more carefully or deliberately ask it several ways and report the spread. I've come to think the spread is itself one of the most interesting findings. It's a measure of how unsettled the concept is in the minds of experts, and that's worth knowing on its own, separately from any particular median year.

r001.rationale: The response says asking respondents how they interpreted questions reveals ambiguity or mistaken assumptions that can explain differing or confusing forecasts and show which results to trust.

astra-6.text:
I think that’s a pretty important part of it, because there can be a surprisingly large gap between what you intended to ask and what someone understood you to be asking. Especially with questions about future AI, where we don’t have very settled concepts, you can get a precise-looking answer without knowing quite what it’s an answer to.

Asking people how they interpreted the question can help distinguish disagreement about the future from disagreement about what the question means. It can also tell us where we should improve the wording next time. I wouldn’t treat their explanations as a perfect window into how they arrived at their answers, but they’re useful evidence. Ideally, you’d do some of that work before running the full survey, so you can catch ambiguities before you’ve collected thousands of answers to them.

r001.rationale: The response says respondents’ interpretations can reveal gaps between intended and understood questions, helping distinguish disagreement about the topic from disagreement about meaning.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that’s quite valuable, because there’s a lot of room for people to interpret these questions differently. If you ask when AI will be able to do every task better and more cheaply than a human, for instance, people might have different ideas about what counts as a task or what conditions they’re supposed to imagine. And those differences can affect their answers quite a lot.

So asking how they understood the question helps us work out what we’re actually measuring. Ideally, you’d do some of that before running the survey, so you can improve the wording. But asking afterward can also help you interpret the results. You don’t want to see a spread of dates and assume it all represents disagreement about how fast AI will progress, when some of it might be people answering different questions.

r001.rationale: The response says asking afterward can help interpret results and identify when varied answers reflect respondents answering different questions, rather than genuine disagreement about AI progress.
